:::{#thm-entropy-at-most-log-values}
#### Entropy is at most the logarithm of the number of values

Let $X$ be a [discrete random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-discrete-rv)
with exactly $k$ [values](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-realization)
of positive [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability).
With base-2 [logarithms](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-logarithm),
the [entropy](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-entropy) of $X$ is at most $\log_2 k$:

$$\entropyf{X} \le \log_2 k,$$

with equality exactly when $X$ is [uniform](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-uniform) on those $k$ values.

:::

::: {.proof}

Let $p$ be the [probability mass function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pmf) of $X$,
and let $q$ be the uniform probability mass function on the $k$ values $x$ with $p(x) > 0$,
so $q(x) = 1/k$ at each of them.
The [surprisal](#def-surprisal) measured by $q$ is then the same at every one of those values:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\surprisalunderf{q}{x}
&= -\log_2 \tfrac{1}{k} \\
&= \log_2 k.
\end{aligned}
$$

The [Kullback--Leibler divergence](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-kl-divergence) of $q$ from $p$
is the [expectation](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-expectation) of the surprisal measured by $q$ minus the surprisal measured by $p$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\kldivf{p}{q}
&= \E{\surprisalunderf{q}{X} - \surprisalf{X}} \\
&= \E{\log_2 k - \surprisalf{X}} \\
&= \log_2 k - \E{\surprisalf{X}} \\
&= \log_2 k - \entropyf{X}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The sum in @thm-kl-divergence-nonnegative has [finitely many](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/functions.html#def-finite-set) terms, so it is finite,
and @thm-kl-divergence-nonnegative then gives $\kldivf{p}{q} \ge 0$,
with equality exactly when $q = p$.
Hence $\log_2 k - \entropyf{X} \ge 0$,
with equality exactly when $p$ is uniform on its $k$ values.

:::
